title: A capital in Damascus
hookLine: the Umayyads rule from Damascus over lands from Spain to Sindh

cards: Put one finger on the Atlantic coast of Spain, where the land runs out into ocean. Put another on the Indus River, in Sindh, in what is now Pakistan. Between your fingers: North Africa, Egypt, Syria, Iraq, Persia.

Under the Umayyad caliphs, one ruling house in Damascus claimed all of it: Arabs, Berbers, Copts, Greeks, Persians and many more, under one government. A new block begins: Islamic history and civilization.

teach.h: A CLAN OF QURAYSH IN DAMASCUS.
teach.b: The Umayyads are a clan of Quraysh, the Prophet's own tribe, and their line of caliphs began with Mu'awiyah, already met on this path, ruling from Damascus. Today the path looks at what that seat became.
Damascus was an old city long before Islam, a crossroads of caravans.

teach.h: WEST TO SPAIN, EAST TO SINDH.
teach.b: From there, Umayyad armies and governors pushed west across North Africa and into Spain, which Muslims called al-Andalus, and east into Central Asia and Sindh.
That's the plain history: an empire, built partly by conquest, with all the costs conquest carries. The people of these lands did not all become Muslim at once.
Churches and synagogues went on, and the histories suggest the change of faith came slowly, family by family. A capital ruling so many peoples has a practical problem: how do you run it?

teach.h: KEEP THE OLD OFFICES, AT FIRST.
teach.b: At first, by keeping the old offices. Clerks in Syria went on keeping records in Greek, as they had under Byzantium. Clerks in Iraq and Persia kept them in Persian.

teach.h: NATIONS AND TRIBES, TO KNOW EACH OTHER.
teach.b: The Qur'an had already spoken to a world of many peoples: "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another."
A capital in Damascus held them under one roof, and from that mix came mosques, coins, books and cities.

how: Muslim histories tell the Umayyad period, ruled from Damascus, as a time of wide expansion, and Sunni and Shia teachers judge its rulers differently.

practice: If you have a map nearby, find Spain and the Indus River and let your eyes travel slowly between them, naming each region as you pass: Morocco, Egypt, Syria, Iraq, Iran.
Then close your eyes and bring to mind the people of those places, then and now: farmers, clerks, merchants, families at prayer in mosques, churches and synagogues.

wordCard.voice: Damascus. The old crossroads city that became the Umayyad capital, from which armies and governors reached from al-Andalus to Sindh. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: from spain to sindh. Nations and tribes, that they may know one another. Until tomorrow.
